opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The basic issue is that misuse risk is only as low as the weakest link in the global ecosystem. Suppose the US and its allies put strong safeguards on frontier models: careful API monitoring, refusals for dangerous bioweapon or cyber requests, restrictions on releasing weights. That helps, but if a comparably capable model is available elsewhere with none of those protections, a malicious actor just goes there. Bad actors don't care which country's model they use. They'll use whichever one gets the job done.

China is the other country with frontier-level capabilities. Its labs are often only months behind, and some of them release very capable open-weight models. So there's no realistic path to keeping dangerous capabilities out of the hands of terrorists or rogue groups that runs only through Western labs. Whatever floor of safety practice you want, it has to hold in China as well, or it doesn't really hold.

I'd also say this is one of the more tractable areas for cooperation, because interests are genuinely aligned. Beijing has no more desire than Washington to see a non-state group synthesize a pandemic pathogen or take down critical infrastructure. That's quite different from questions about military AI or economic competition, where the two sides really are adversaries. Misuse by third parties is a shared threat, a bit like nuclear security, where the US and Soviet Union cooperated on keeping fissile material away from terrorists even at the height of the Cold War.

Concretely, that could mean agreeing on what counts as a dangerous capability, sharing evaluation methods so both sides measure risk the same way, setting norms around when model weights shouldn't be released, and coordinating on things like DNA synthesis screening. None of it requires trusting each other on everything. It only requires recognizing that on this specific problem, neither side can solve it alone.

r001.rationale: The response says actors would turn to capable models without safeguards, including open-weight models, but does not predict that most remaining misuse risk would shift toward open-weight models after widespread adoption of strong safeguards at American companies.

r002.rationale: It identifies China as a source of capable open-weight models and says dangerous capabilities cannot be kept from misuse through Western labs alone.

r003.rationale: It describes preventing non-state groups from using AI to create a pathogen or attack infrastructure as a threat shared by Beijing and Washington.

r004.rationale: It proposes sharing evaluation methods and agreeing on norms, but does not connect scientific agreement on AI safety to generating political will.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the basic point is that AI misuse isn't a problem that respects borders. If we're worried about, say, a bio-weapons attack enabled by a frontier model, it doesn't really matter whether that model was trained in San Francisco or Shenzhen. The pathogen is just as dangerous either way. And China is one of only two countries right now that's genuinely at the frontier of this technology. So if we implement really strong safeguards in the US and in Europe, but there are capable open-weight models coming out of Chinese labs with no comparable restrictions, then a lot of our effort is just being undercut. Bad actors will route around whatever controls we've put in place.

The second thing I'd say is that there's actually a lot of shared interest here that I think gets obscured by the competitive framing. The Chinese government does not want non-state actors with bioweapons. They don't want cyberattacks on their critical infrastructure. They have, if anything, a stronger institutional preference for control and stability than most Western governments do. So when it comes to misuse specifically, as distinct from questions about who gets the economic or military advantage, the interests are really quite aligned. That's a different situation from, say, trying to coordinate on slowing down capabilities, where you really do run into a prisoner's dilemma.

And then there's a precedent here. We've done this before with nuclear non-proliferation, with bioweapons conventions, with things like the hotline between Washington and Moscow at the height of the Cold War. These were adversaries who had deep, fundamental disagreements but still managed to cooperate on a narrow set of catastrophic risks because both sides recognized that it was in their interest. I don't think it's naive to think we can do something similar with AI. What I think is naive is assuming we can get a good outcome on misuse purely unilaterally.

Now, I want to be realistic about this. There's a lot of distrust, there are export controls, there's a geopolitical competition that's not going away. I'm not suggesting we hand over model weights or share anything that creates a security vulnerability. But things like agreeing on common evaluation standards for dangerous capabilities, sharing information about incidents, having technical dialogues between researchers, those are low-cost, high-value, and they build the kind of channels you need to have in place before a crisis, not during one. If we wait until something goes badly wrong to start talking, we'll have left it far too late.

r001.rationale: The response says Chinese open-weight models could undercut US and European safeguards, but it does not predict that most remaining misuse risk would shift to open-weight models.

r002.rationale: It identifies Chinese labs as a source of capable open-weight models and says those models could let bad actors route around US and European controls, making unilateral action inadequate.

r003.rationale: It describes preventing non-state actors from obtaining bioweapons as an interest shared with China, in the context of AI misuse risks such as AI-enabled bioweapon attacks.

r004.rationale: It recommends common evaluation standards and technical dialogue, but does not call for scientific agreement on AI safety to generate political will.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic reason is that misuse is a global problem. If you’re worried about someone using AI to develop a biological weapon or carry out a major cyberattack, safeguards put in place by American companies only get you so far. If a similarly capable system is available elsewhere without those safeguards, a malicious actor can simply use that one.

So you need some degree of cooperation among the countries developing these systems, and China is clearly one of those countries. That doesn’t mean we have to agree on everything, or share all of our technology. It means finding areas where our interests overlap. Neither country wants powerful AI tools to enable terrorism or attacks on critical infrastructure.

There are real questions about trust and verification. But I’d distinguish those challenges from whether cooperation is necessary. We can compete in many respects while still trying to establish a baseline of safeguards against misuse that would threaten both countries.

r001.rationale: The response says American safeguards can be bypassed by using a similarly capable system elsewhere, but does not predict that widespread safeguards would shift most remaining risk toward open-weight models.

r002.rationale: It identifies China as a country developing AI systems, but does not call China a major source of open-weight models.

r003.rationale: The response says neither country wants AI to enable terrorism and presents overlapping interests as a basis for cooperation.

r004.rationale: The response discusses cooperation and safeguards but does not call for scientific agreement on safety to translate into political will.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic reason is that AI misuse is a global problem. If we develop safeguards in the United States, but someone can get essentially the same capabilities from a model developed in China without those safeguards, then we haven’t really solved the problem. We’ve just changed where they go to access those capabilities.

That doesn’t mean we need to agree with China on everything, or share sensitive technical information. But there are areas where there should be a common interest: neither country wants terrorist groups to have access to tools that help them develop biological weapons, for example. So I think there’s room for fairly narrow cooperation around identifying those risks, evaluating models, and establishing some basic expectations for preventing misuse.

Verification is going to be difficult, and we shouldn’t assume that an agreement on paper is sufficient. But if we want safeguards to actually be effective internationally, we need some way of bringing the major AI developers into that conversation, including those in China.

r001.rationale: The response says safeguards in the U.S. could leave equivalent capabilities available from Chinese models, but it does not predict that widespread proprietary safeguards would shift most remaining risk toward open-weight models.

r002.rationale: It mentions models developed in China, but does not identify China as a major source of open-weight models or connect that role to the limits of U.S.-only action.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says neither country wants terrorist groups to access AI tools that could help develop biological weapons, presenting this as a shared basis for narrow cooperation.

r004.rationale: The response calls for cooperation and basic expectations, but does not call for scientific agreement on AI safety to translate into political will.
